In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
1. Abstinence is not the main problem in HIV prevention.

(i) HIV transmission is a function of both individual and contextual factors, (ii) the individual factors include the frequency and nature of sexual contacts, the use or non-use of condoms, and other sexual practices, (iii) the contextual factors include poverty and inequality, gender, and cultural factors, (iv) the balance between individual and contextual factors varies between settings, and (v) the balance between the two is changing over time.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social context of sexual behaviour, including the availability and acceptability of condoms, is the most important influence on the likelihood of transmission, not individual choice or behaviour.
the current focus on "behavior change" is misguided.
the "abstinence only" message has no place in the prevention of HIV/AIDS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to understand the social context within which people make their decisions about sexual behaviour, and that the social context is often more important than the individual.
the "abstinence-only" approach is not a reasonable goal of HIV/AIDS prevention, and that the focus on behaviour change alone as a solution to the epidemic is misguided.
